content:
Amazon Transcribe vs OpenAI Whisper: Which Speech-to-Text Solution Is Better Suited to Vietnamese? Speech-to-Text (STT) technology is increasingly common, from automatic video captions and meeting transcripts to customer support call analysis. Two notable solutions are Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper. Both convert audio into text, but they differ significantly in their deployment models, capabilities, pricing structures, and operational requirements.
These differences are particularly relevant for Vietnamese, a tonal language with regional accents and frequent mixing of Vietnamese and English technical terms. Choosing the wrong service can lead to low transcription accuracy, unexpected operational costs, or excessive infrastructure maintenance.
This article provides a comprehensive comparison of the two options across speech recognition capabilities, Vietnamese language support, deployment models, cost analysis, practical architectures, evaluation metrics, and real-world decision guidance.
1. Overview of Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper Amazon Transcribe Amazon Transcribe is an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) service from AWS. It converts audio into text without requiring developers to build or operate their own machine learning model.
As a fully managed service, AWS maintains the underlying infrastructure, speech recognition models, scaling, and updates. The application provides audio input and the necessary processing configuration.
Amazon Transcribe offers two main processing modes:
Batch Transcription: Transcribes existing audio recordings stored in Amazon S3. Suitable for offline processing of lectures, interviews, and call center recordings. Streaming Transcription: Transcribes incoming audio with near-real-time results. Suitable for live captioning, virtual assistants, and real-time meeting assistants. Depending on the language, the service also provides features such as Custom Vocabulary, Speaker Diarization, Language Identification, Content Redaction, and Call Analytics.
Its ability to integrate with Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS Step Functions, and other AWS services makes it useful for automated audio-processing workflows without managing servers.
OpenAI Whisper Whisper is an open-source speech recognition model introduced by OpenAI in 2022. It uses a Transformer architecture and was trained on approximately 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervised data collected from the web.
Whisper supports multilingual speech transcription, language detection, and translation of speech into English.
It is available in several model sizes, including Tiny, Base, Small, Medium, Large-v1, Large-v2, Large-v3, and Turbo, with different compute requirements and performance trade-offs.
Unlike Amazon Transcribe, the open-source model can run locally or on cloud infrastructure such as Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, or Amazon EKS.
This gives developers control over the runtime environment, model selection, versioning, and data processing. In exchange, they must manage the computing resources, dependencies, model weights, application infrastructure, security patches, and scaling themselves.
Figure 2. OpenAI Whisper’s Transformer encoder-decoder architecture for multilingual speech recognition. Source: OpenAI GitHub.
2. Vietnamese Speech Recognition Capabilities Vietnamese is a tonal language with six tones, rich diacritics, regional accents (Northern, Central, Southern), and frequent code-switching between Vietnamese and English technical terms. Noisy recordings and unclear pronunciation make accurate transcription more difficult.
Vietnamese Support in Amazon Transcribe According to AWS documentation referenced for this post, Amazon Transcribe supports Vietnamese (vi-VN) in both batch and streaming modes.
Custom Vocabulary is useful for adding names, product terms, and domain-specific terminology to improve recognition accuracy for Vietnamese technical conversations.
However, Vietnamese was not supported by Amazon Transcribe’s automatic Language Identification feature in the referenced language support table. Applications processing Vietnamese audio should therefore specify vi-VN explicitly rather than relying on auto-detection.
Custom Language Models and some advanced analysis features were also unavailable for Vietnamese in that language support information at the time of publication.
Vietnamese Support in Whisper Whisper supports Vietnamese through its multilingual models. It can detect the input language automatically or be configured to use a specified language code (vi).
Its diverse audio training data provides a basis for handling various speakers and recording conditions, although the model does not produce perfect results in every setting.
For example, consider the sentence:
“Hôm nay sẽ deploy ứng dụng lên Amazon EC2, sau đó cấu hình Security Group và kết nối với RDS.”
English technical terms such as “deploy”, “Security Group”, and “RDS” may be misrecognized when pronunciation is unclear or background noise is present.
With Amazon Transcribe, Custom Vocabulary is one possible way to improve recognition of technical expressions. With Whisper, developers can experiment with different model sizes (Large-v3 typically performs best) and context prompts where supported.
Without a common benchmark dataset, it would be misleading to claim that either system is consistently more accurate for Vietnamese. A fair comparison should cover Northern, Central, and Southern accents, audio quality (telephony vs. studio), background noise levels, and different speaking scenarios (formal presentations vs. casual conversations).
3. Deployment Cost Comparison Cost matters, particularly for applications that process hundreds or thousands of hours of audio.
Amazon Transcribe Amazon Transcribe uses pay-as-you-go pricing based on the processed audio duration.
Using an illustrative first-tier Standard Transcription rate of USD 0.024 per minute in US East (N. Virginia), processing ten hours of audio would cost approximately USD 14.40.
Actual charges depend on AWS Region, pricing tiers, optional features (such as speaker diarization or content redaction), and additional services such as S3 storage and Lambda invocations.
A key benefit is that the application does not have to keep a GPU server running or manage the ASR model. This can be valuable when workloads are irregular or unpredictable.
OpenAI Whisper The open-source Whisper model has no model license fee, but inference still requires computing resources.
When deployed on Amazon EC2, costs depend on instance type, runtime duration, storage, data transfer, and performance requirements.
Whisper can run on CPUs, but larger models (Large-v2, Large-v3) typically require GPUs for acceptable inference speed. GPUs can speed up inference in many scenarios, at the cost of more expensive infrastructure.
For applications processing just a few recordings each day, keeping a GPU instance online continuously may be inefficient. On the other hand, existing infrastructure or Spot Instances that can be started only when needed may make self-hosting worthwhile.
The open-source model should not be confused with the hosted OpenAI Whisper API. The whisper-1 API is a separately billed service, and OpenAI announced its discontinuation for February 26, 2027. This does not discontinue the open-source Whisper model.
A fair cost comparison therefore needs to include compute, storage, operations, maintenance, scalability, and engineering time—not just a price per audio minute.
Summary Table Factor Amazon Transcribe OpenAI Whisper (self-hosted) Pricing model Pay per audio minute Compute instance cost + engineering time Infrastructure Fully managed by AWS Self-managed on EC2/ECS/EKS GPU required No Recommended for Large models Scaling Automatic Manual or Auto Scaling group Model updates Managed by AWS Manual version management Data residency Configurable AWS Region Full control over deployment location 4. Practical Use Case: Turning Lectures into Text A useful Speech-to-Text application is a service that automatically converts recorded lectures to searchable transcripts. Students can look up key passages, extract information, or generate summaries rather than listening to the entire recording again.
Both Amazon Transcribe and Whisper can support this workflow.
Option A: Amazon Transcribe The architecture can combine Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon Transcribe:
A user uploads an audio file to Amazon S3. The upload event triggers AWS Lambda. Lambda starts a Transcription Job with the language code vi-VN. Amazon Transcribe processes the audio and produces the transcript. The transcript is stored in S3 for the application to retrieve. This approach uses managed AWS services and requires no self-hosted speech recognition model.
Option B: Whisper on Amazon EC2 The architecture can combine Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, and Amazon EC2:
An audio recording is uploaded to S3. A processing request is sent to an Amazon SQS queue. An EC2 worker receives the request and downloads the audio. Whisper transcribes the recording into Vietnamese text. The result is saved to Amazon S3. The second option requires direct control of the inference environment, but makes it possible to choose the Whisper version, configure compute resources, and optimize the pipeline.
Either solution could later include automatic lecture summarization using an LLM through Amazon Bedrock.
5. How Should Accuracy Be Evaluated? A few individual recordings are not enough to evaluate a Speech-to-Text system fairly.
A useful test dataset could include:
Recordings of speakers from different Vietnamese regions (Northern, Central, Southern). Clear studio-quality recordings and recordings with background noise. Everyday conversations and conversations containing technical vocabulary. Code-switched Vietnamese-English technical discussions. The same dataset should then be processed by both services and compared against human-verified reference transcripts.
Two common evaluation metrics are:
Word Error Rate (WER): Measures recognition errors at the word level compared with a reference transcript.
Character Error Rate (CER): Measures recognition errors at the character level.
Lower values generally indicate better recognition under the selected metric. For Vietnamese, a consistent text normalization procedure (handling diacritics, case, and punctuation) is important before calculating the scores.
Processing time, cost per audio hour, and operational complexity should also be considered. A small accuracy gain may not justify substantially higher infrastructure costs for every application.
6. When Should Each Solution Be Considered? Amazon Transcribe is a practical option for applications already using AWS, especially when the goal is to deliver a speech transcription feature quickly without maintaining the ML infrastructure.
Its near-real-time Vietnamese streaming support and integration with other AWS services are significant advantages.
Self-hosted Whisper is worth considering for research, custom inference workflows, or environments where direct control of model deployment, versioning, and data handling is important.
However, hardware requirements, model versioning, and ongoing operations should be evaluated carefully before choosing a self-hosted deployment.
7. Conclusion Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper address the same Speech-to-Text problem with different approaches.
Amazon Transcribe provides a managed recognition service, reducing deployment and operations work. The open-source Whisper model offers greater flexibility and control over the runtime and model configuration.
Both support Vietnamese, but comparative accuracy needs to be tested on the same input data rather than assumed.
The right decision depends on transcript quality, cost, performance, scalability, and operational requirements. A useful next step would be to benchmark both solutions against a Vietnamese dataset containing multiple regional accents and recording conditions.

title: Create a gateway endpoint

Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Worklog
Blog 2
content:
From Meeting Transcripts to Notion Tasks: When DynamoDB Streams, Lambda, and Bedrock Work Together Having a complete transcript after a meeting does not necessarily solve the follow-up problem. A transcript might contain thousands of words, while the most useful information is often much simpler: Who is responsible for which task? What is the deadline? Which action items still need attention?
Manually listening to recordings, reading through long transcripts, deciding what needs to be done, writing it down, and creating tasks in a project management tool is time-consuming and error-prone. Important items get forgotten, deadlines are missed, and context is lost between the meeting and the task tracker.
One practical approach is to combine Amazon DynamoDB Streams, AWS Lambda, and Amazon Bedrock to extract action items automatically and synchronize them with Notion. This post walks through the architecture, implementation considerations, a Python code example, idempotency strategies, human-in-the-loop confirmation, cost considerations, and how to extend the pattern to other tools.
1. How Does the Architecture Work? Imagine that someone says during a meeting:
“Lan will finish the login API by October 30.”
After the meeting ends, the system can follow this workflow:
Amazon DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams The backend updates the meeting status to COMPLETED in DynamoDB. DynamoDB Streams captures the data change, and AWS Lambda can be configured to process the stream event.
The useful separation here is that the backend does not need to invoke the entire AI workflow directly. Post-meeting analysis can run independently, and the main application remains responsive.
AWS Lambda Lambda acts as the coordinator. It receives the stream event, retrieves the corresponding transcript from Amazon S3, and prepares the content for AI processing.
Instead of copying a long transcript into Notion, the Lambda function asks a model available through Amazon Bedrock to identify relevant action items.
Amazon Bedrock The language model turns conversational content into structured data. For example:
Task: Complete the login API Assignee: Lan Deadline: October 30 Source: The relevant transcript segment After receiving the response, Lambda validates the data and calls the Notion API to create an item in a task database.
Why This Design Works Event-driven: No polling. The pipeline starts automatically when meeting metadata changes in DynamoDB. Serverless: No EC2 instances to manage. You pay only for the compute and API calls you actually use. Decoupled: Transcript storage, AI extraction, and task creation are separate concerns. You can replace Bedrock with another model, or Notion with another task tool, without rewriting the whole pipeline. Observable: Each step emits logs and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, making failures easy to debug. 2. How It Works Step by Step Step 1: Meeting Metadata Lands in DynamoDB When a meeting finishes, an item is written (or updated) in a DynamoDB table called Meetings:
meeting_id (PK) status transcript_s3_url created_at mtg-2026-10-28-001 completed s3://meeting-transcripts/mtg-001.txt 2026-10-28T10:00:00Z The status field moves from pending to completed. DynamoDB Streams captures this change.
Step 2: Lambda Extracts Action Items with Bedrock A Lambda function (process-meeting-transcript) is triggered by the stream. It:
Reads the meeting_id and transcript_s3_url from the stream record. Downloads the transcript from S3. Calls Amazon Bedrock with a prompt such as: You are an assistant that extracts action items from meeting transcripts.
Transcript: {{transcript}}
Return a JSON array of action items. Each item must have: title, description, assignee, due_date, priority. Only include items that are clearly actionable. Ignore general discussion.
Parses the JSON response from Bedrock. Step 3: Human Confirmation Before creating tasks in Notion, the extracted action items are paused for review. Options include:
Storing proposed tasks in a ProposedTasks DynamoDB table with status = pending_review. Sending a notification (Slack, email, or internal dashboard) with the proposed tasks and Approve/Reject buttons. Only writing to Notion after an approver marks the item as approved. Step 4: Create Tasks in Notion Once confirmed, a Lambda function calls the Notion API (POST https://api.notion.com/v1/pages) to create a page in the Notion database:
Title: Action item title Assignee: Person responsible Due date: When it should be completed Priority: High / Medium / Low Related meeting: Link back to the original meeting record Step 5: Idempotency To avoid creating duplicate tasks if the Lambda is retried or the stream event is delivered twice:
Each proposed task set is stored with a unique meeting_id + batch_id key. Before writing to Notion, the function checks whether tasks for this meeting_id already exist in the ProposedTasks table. Notion page creation records the notion_page_id back to DynamoDB so the same meeting is not processed again. Figure 2. DynamoDB stream shards and AWS Lambda event processing. Source: AWS Database Blog.
3. Example: Lambda Handler (Python) import json import boto3 import os from botocore.exceptions import ClientError s3 = boto3.client("s3") bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime") dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb") MODEL_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_MODEL_ID", "anthropic.claude-3-sonnet-20240229-v1:0") NOTION_DATABASE_ID = os.environ["NOTION_DATABASE_ID"] NOTION_API_KEY = os.environ["NOTION_API_KEY"] PROPOSED_TABLE = os.environ["PROPOSED_TASKS_TABLE"] def extract_action_items(transcript: str) -> list: prompt = f"""Extract action items from this meeting transcript. Return ONLY a JSON array. Each item: {{"title": "...", "description": "...", "assignee": "...", "due_date": "...", "priority": "High|Medium|Low"}} Transcript: {transcript}""" response = bedrock.invoke_model( modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 1000, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] }) ) result = json.loads(response["body"].read()) return json.loads(result["content"][0]["text"]) def save_proposed_tasks(meeting_id: str, items: list): table = dynamodb.Table(PROPOSED_TABLE) table.put_item(Item={ "meeting_id": meeting_id, "status": "pending_review", "items": items, "created_at": json.dumps({"__type": "timestamp", "iso": str(__import__("datetime").datetime.utcnow())}) }) def already_processed(meeting_id: str) -> bool: table = dynamodb.Table(PROPOSED_TABLE) resp = table.get_item(Key={"meeting_id": meeting_id}) return "Item" in resp def lambda_handler(event, context): for record in event["Records"]: if record["eventName"] not in ("INSERT", "MODIFY"): continue meeting_id = record["dynamodb"]["Keys"]["meeting_id"]["S"] status = record["dynamodb"]["NewImage"].get("status", {}).get("S") s3_url = record["dynamodb"]["NewImage"].get("transcript_s3_url", {}).get("S") if status != "completed" or not s3_url: continue # Idempotency check if already_processed(meeting_id): continue bucket, key = parse_s3_url(s3_url) transcript = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)["Body"].read().decode("utf-8") items = extract_action_items(transcript) # Pause for human confirmation before writing to Notion save_proposed_tasks(meeting_id, items) # After confirmation (separate step), call create_notion_tasks(items) return {"statusCode": 200} 4. Idempotency and Human Confirmation Concern How it is handled Duplicate processing DynamoDB table stores processed_meeting_ids; Lambda checks before creating Notion tasks. Stream redelivery Same meeting_id produces the same proposed tasks; Notion creation is gated behind confirmation. Wrong task created Human review step lets an approver edit or reject items before they reach Notion. Partial failure Proposed tasks are stored in DynamoDB first; Notion creation is a separate, retryable step. LLM hallucination Fields not clearly supported by the transcript remain empty rather than being inferred. 5. Cost Considerations Amazon S3: Pay per GB stored and per request. Transcripts are small text files, so cost is negligible. DynamoDB: Pay per read/write request and storage. Ideal for lightweight meeting metadata. AWS Lambda: Pay per invocation and duration. Short Python functions keep cost low. Amazon Bedrock: Pay per input/output token processed by the model. Long transcripts cost more; consider summarizing very long transcripts before sending to Bedrock. Notion API: Free tier is available for small teams; paid plans for higher limits. 6. Extending the Pattern The same architecture can be extended to:
Jira, Asana, Trello, or ClickUp: Replace the Notion API call with the respective task tool API. Email transcripts: Replace S3 + DynamoDB with an SES inbound email handler. Call center transcripts: Replace meeting audio with contact center recordings from Amazon Connect. Scheduled reports: Add a weekly Lambda that scans all pending_review items and sends a summary email. 7. Conclusion This architecture turns meeting transcripts into structured, trackable work without manual copy-paste. By combining DynamoDB Streams, AWS Lambda, Amazon Bedrock, and the Notion API, you get a serverless pipeline that:
Starts automatically when a meeting ends. Extracts action items using generative AI. Keeps humans in the loop before tasks are created. Avoids duplicates with idempotency checks. The same pattern can be extended to other document sources (email, support tickets, call center transcripts) and other task destinations (Jira, Asana, Trello, or a custom database).
References AWS – DynamoDB Streams and Lambda Triggers Amazon Bedrock – Structured Outputs Notion – Create a Page API AWS Lambda – Documentation Bài viết đã đăng trên AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2318521822246110/?rdid=ZaQ8iG8gfsmGlEWb#

title: Proposal
content:
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator .
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File .
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

title: Blog 3
content:
Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic – When a Voice Agent Can Do More Than Talk An AI voice assistant is often described as a three-stage pipeline: convert speech to text (Speech-to-Text), send the text to an LLM, and convert the answer back to audio (Text-to-Speech).
This design is familiar and straightforward. However, chaining different components can increase latency in real-time conversations. It also introduces challenges when a user interrupts a response, changes the question, or asks the assistant to carry out an action.
On October 5, 2026, AWS announced Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a new speech-to-speech model available through Amazon Bedrock, designed for natural real-time conversations and task execution through connected tools.
The interesting aspect is not only voice generation and understanding but also how the model can work with AWS services to create a complete voice agent.
1. What Makes Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic Different? Instead of requiring a separate STT → LLM → TTS pipeline, Nova 2.5 Sonic can take audio input and generate audio output within the same model.
AWS has also improved reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling capabilities compared with Nova 2 Sonic.
Several features stand out:
Real-time speech-to-speech: Two-way voice interactions with low latency. Barge-in: Users can interrupt the agent while it is speaking. Tool calling: The model can request that the application call an API to retrieve information or perform an action. Asynchronous tool calling: The conversation does not always have to stop completely while external tools are running. Cross-modal interaction: Voice and text can be combined in the same session. Tool calling and barge-in are particularly important for voice agents used in real applications.
2. Combining Nova Sonic with AWS Services One possible architecture combines Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime provides a runtime for agents and can support bidirectional WebSocket communication for transmitting and receiving audio. This allows developers to use a managed agent runtime rather than building the entire session infrastructure themselves.
Within the runtime, Strands BidiAgent can manage the conversation session, communicate with Nova Sonic, and handle tool requests.
Amazon Bedrock Amazon Bedrock provides the Nova 2.5 Sonic model, which interprets speech, maintains conversation context, and generates responses.
AgentCore Gateway and AWS Lambda When the agent needs external data, AgentCore Gateway can provide access to MCP-based tools. Behind the gateway, AWS Lambda handles business logic while Amazon DynamoDB stores application data.
The model therefore does not need unrestricted direct access to the database. Business APIs can enforce authorization, validation, and other safeguards.
Supporting Services Amazon S3: Optional audio archive for recorded sessions. Amazon CloudWatch: Logs, traces, and metrics for observability. Amazon Cognito: User sign-in / JWT / temporary credentials for identity and access. Figure 2. AgentCore Runtime architecture for bidirectional voice interactions using Amazon Nova Sonic. Source: AWS Documentation.
3. The Interesting Part: Talking and Completing Tasks Consider a customer-service voice agent.
A customer asks:
“Can you check my latest order?”
The agent invokes a tool to check order status. While the system is retrieving that information, the customer adds:
“Actually, can I change the delivery address?”
A well-designed agent must preserve context, understand the new request, and identify the necessary actions.
If an address change is possible, it can request the corresponding API. However, any actual update must follow access controls, business rules, and appropriate confirmation steps.
This separates an AI system that merely speaks from a voice agent that can interact with external systems.
Another example is when an agent is explaining a delivery policy and the user interrupts:
“Just tell me when it arrives.”
Barge-in support helps the application respond to this interruption rather than forcing the user to listen to the entire previous answer.
Key Capabilities of a Production Voice Agent A production-ready AI Agent requires more than a Large Language Model. Important components include:
LLM: Processes requests and generates responses. Runtime: Provides an environment in which the Agent can execute. Tools and APIs: Allow the Agent to interact with external systems. Memory and Context: Help retain relevant information across interactions. Security and Guardrails: Restrict unsafe operations and protect sensitive resources. Monitoring and Cost Management: Help track usage, performance, and operating expenses. 4. Should Nova 2.5 Sonic Be Used for Every Audio Application? Not necessarily.
Nova 2.5 Sonic is more suited to live voice interaction, such as customer support, appointment scheduling, and spoken information retrieval.
For a workflow that simply converts a recorded audio file into text for storage or later analysis, Amazon Transcribe remains a reasonable option.
AWS lists seven supported languages for Nova 2.5 Sonic, and Vietnamese was not on the officially supported list at the time of this post. This is an important limitation for applications serving Vietnamese-speaking users.
The overall cost is not limited to model usage. AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other infrastructure components may add operating costs.
5. Conclusion The important shift illustrated by Nova 2.5 Sonic is the move from voice assistants to voice agents.
Rather than only listening and responding, the system can maintain a conversation, retrieve information, and invoke authorized tools to carry out tasks.
Combining Nova Sonic with AgentCore and other AWS services offers developers a practical approach to building real-time conversational applications without managing every part of the agent infrastructure on their own.
This direction is worth exploring as AI applications evolve from answering questions to helping users complete real work.

title: Blogs Posted
content:
During my internship at AWS First Cloud AI Journey, I spent time researching articles from the AWS Blog, combining hands-on lab experience and daily learning to write technical blog posts. Each blog post focuses on a specific topic, helping me consolidate knowledge, share experiences, and introduce solutions and best practices on AWS. My goal is to contribute practical, accessible content to the AWS Study Group community that can be applied directly to real-world work.
The following blog posts were shared on AWS Study Group:
Blog 1 - Amazon Transcribe vs OpenAI Whisper: Which Speech-to-Text Solution Fits Vietnamese? Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper approach the same speech-to-text problem from two different directions: a fully managed AWS service and an open-source model that teams can self-host. The post compares Vietnamese recognition quality, deployment models, operating costs, and the trade-offs between convenience and control. It also walks through practical AWS architectures, from batch transcription to near-real-time streaming, and explains how to evaluate results objectively with Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER). Rather than assuming one option is better, the article shows how to benchmark both solutions on the same Vietnamese dataset and choose based on accuracy, budget, and operational requirements.
Blog 2 - From Meeting Transcripts to Notion Tasks with DynamoDB Streams, Lambda and Bedrock The post describes an event-driven pipeline that starts automatically when a meeting transcript is marked as completed in DynamoDB. DynamoDB Streams triggers AWS Lambda, which reads the transcript from Amazon S3, calls Amazon Bedrock to extract action items, and stores the proposed tasks for human review before creating them in Notion. The article explains each step in detail, including the Lambda handler, prompt design, idempotency checks, human confirmation, and cost considerations. It also discusses how the same pattern can be extended to email, support tickets, call-center transcripts, and other task management tools, making it a reusable blueprint for serverless automation.
Blog 3 - Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic: From Voice Assistants to Task-Performing Voice Agents The post examines Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model on Amazon Bedrock that aims to replace the traditional STT → LLM → TTS pipeline with a single real-time model. It covers low-latency voice interaction, barge-in, tool calling, asynchronous tool use, and cross-modal sessions, then shows how Nova Sonic can be combined with AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to build a complete voice agent. The article also discusses practical use cases, current language limitations, cost and operational considerations, and when a simpler transcription service such as Amazon Transcribe is still the better choice.

Event Takeaways: “AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day” Event Objectives Learn how engineering teams approach software development at scale, including the practical challenges of building Software Factories. Explore the skills students need to bridge academic learning and real-world Cloud and software engineering work. Understand the ideas presented in the AWS Lambda Web Functions session, particularly HTTP handling, request concurrency, performance and cost considerations. Explore how Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) can decouple components and support asynchronous system design. Learn from an AWS internship journey and explore ways to begin and maintain contributions to open-source projects. Connect the technical topics to future Cloud projects and professional development. Speakers The event poster introduced six speakers from industry and the FCAJ community:
Thinh Nguyen – STYL Solutions. Henry Duc Bui – CloudThinker. Hung Tran – NAB. Dao Cu Long – FCAJ. Khang Duong – FCAJ. Tuan Tran – FCAJ. The event was scheduled for 9:00 AM–12:00 PM on Saturday, October 31, 2026, at the 26th floor of Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City.
Key Highlights Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories (9:00–9:25 AM) The session focused on practical lessons from building Software Factories at scale rather than treating software delivery as a series of isolated coding tasks. Its agenda highlighted common implementation pitfalls and the importance of identifying approaches that work in real engineering teams. A useful topic for further study is how standardized workflows, automation and feedback loops support predictable software delivery. The session provides a reason to examine maintainability and developer experience alongside deployment speed. Education (9:30–9:55 AM) This session examined how students can prepare for Cloud and software engineering careers from an educator’s perspective. It addressed the gap between university learning and expectations in the workplace. Technical fundamentals, hands-on projects, communication and independent problem-solving are all relevant areas for students to reflect on. The discussion topic emphasizes that completing tutorials is different from explaining design decisions and working within a team. AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture (10:00–10:25 AM) The session introduced an approach to Serverless web applications involving native HTTP support and multi-concurrency of up to 128 requests, as described in the event agenda. It raised the question of when a Serverless approach can reduce adapter overhead compared with alternative deployment patterns. Active CPU Billing was included as a topic for analyzing cost efficiency rather than considering only the number of invocations. Performance benchmarking against container-based workloads on Amazon EC2 or Amazon ECS was part of the announced session scope. The key architectural question is how latency, request patterns, scaling behavior and total operating costs affect platform selection. Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems (10:30–11:00 AM) Amazon SQS was presented as a building block for asynchronous processing and decoupling services. Queues allow work to be buffered rather than requiring every request to be completed immediately by a downstream component. A practical design should account for retries, visibility timeouts, duplicate messages and dead-letter queues where appropriate. An example is a file-processing application: the upload service receives a file, while workers independently process queued tasks. The session topic illustrates how asynchronous design can improve resilience and help systems handle fluctuating workloads. My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey (11:00–11:25 AM) This session shared a three-month internship perspective, including the use of AWS services in a real project. A relevant lesson is to connect technical exercises with clear project objectives and measurable outcomes. Cloud projects involve more than launching resources: security, monitoring, documentation, cost and troubleshooting also matter. The session offered a useful context for reviewing learning progress and preparing for the transition from university projects to professional work. Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing (11:30 AM–12:00 PM) The session focused on how to begin contributing to open-source projects and maintain a consistent contribution habit. Contributions can start with documentation, issue reproduction, small bug fixes or tests instead of large feature implementations. Reviewing contribution guidelines and working with Git branches and pull requests are practical skills to develop. Regular, manageable contributions can help build familiarity with collaborative software development and code review. What I Learned Software Engineering and Career Preparation A sustainable software delivery process needs clear conventions, repeatable workflows and feedback, not only faster coding. Engineering skills grow when academic concepts are applied to practical systems and their trade-offs can be explained. Internship projects should be documented with their goals, architecture, technical decisions and results. Serverless Architecture and Cost Awareness Serverless design choices should be evaluated using workload characteristics such as request volume, execution time, concurrency and latency. Performance benchmarks need comparable conditions before conclusions can be drawn about AWS Lambda, EC2 or ECS. Cost analysis should include more than the advertised compute rate: supporting services, operational overhead and idle capacity can influence the final result. The Lambda Web Functions claims in the agenda are useful starting points for further documentation review and hands-on validation. Asynchronous Processing with Amazon SQS A queue separates the rate at which requests arrive from the rate at which workers process them. Producers and consumers can be scaled and deployed independently when the application is designed around a queue. Reliability requires thoughtful handling of retries, idempotency, failed messages and monitoring of queue depth. Asynchronous processing is particularly relevant for workloads such as video conversion, background notifications and audio transcription. Open Source and Continuous Learning Small, consistent contributions are a practical way to gain experience with real codebases. Reading existing code and documentation is an important part of contributing effectively. Technical growth also depends on communication, collaboration and the habit of evaluating lessons from completed work. Applying to Work Review project development workflows for opportunities to automate testing, builds, deployment and documentation. Compare Serverless and EC2/ECS deployment options using realistic request patterns, latency targets and cost assumptions. Explore Amazon SQS for asynchronous tasks that do not need to complete within the user-facing HTTP request. Design background workers with retry handling, visibility timeouts, idempotency and dead-letter queue policies. Apply the event’s Cloud engineering themes to project documentation: explain the architecture, permissions, monitoring and operational trade-offs. Build a sustainable open-source learning routine, beginning with small, reviewable contributions. Event Experience The AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day brought together software engineering, Cloud architecture and professional development topics in one morning. The program combined industry perspectives with sessions relevant to students preparing for Cloud and software development roles.
Connecting Architecture with Real-World Decisions The Software Factories session raised questions about the processes required to develop and maintain software at scale. The AWS Lambda Web Functions topic connected Serverless architecture with performance measurement and cost evaluation. The Amazon SQS topic showed why communication patterns matter when applications grow beyond a single service. Connecting Learning with Professional Practice The Education and internship sessions highlighted the importance of hands-on learning and explaining technical choices. The open-source topic provided a concrete direction for practicing team workflows outside the classroom. Together, these themes encourage a balance between technical depth and steady professional development. Networking and Personal Development The program offered an opportunity to engage with AWS and software engineering topics from different professional perspectives. Its mixture of technical and career-focused sessions offers useful directions for further study, particularly distributed systems and developer workflows. Specific discussion points and personal observations can be added here from event notes before the final report is submitted. Lessons Learned Engineering is more than code: processes and collaboration influence how software is delivered. Evaluate Serverless with evidence: latency, concurrency and cost should be measured for the target workload. Decoupling supports scalability: asynchronous queues help separate components and smooth workload spikes. Operational details matter: retries, monitoring and failure handling are essential in production systems. Internships connect theory and practice: real projects require architectural reasoning and clear communication. Consistency supports growth: regular open-source contributions can strengthen long-term engineering skills. Some Event Photos AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day (third person from the right).
Overall, AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day offered an opportunity to connect software delivery practices, Serverless design, asynchronous processing and career preparation. The sessions provide useful directions for further exploration: comparing Cloud architectures with measurable criteria, using queues where asynchronous processing is appropriate, documenting AWS internship projects carefully and developing a consistent approach to open-source learning.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Workshop
content:
Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
